Both articles report the identical set of nine JEPs (523, 527, 531, 532, 533, 534, 536, 537, 538), the identical headline facts (G1 as universal default GC, post-quantum hybrid TLS 1.3 key exchange with the same three named schemes, compact object headers on by default with the same SPECjbb2015/GC/JSON-parser benchmark figures), and overlapping primary sources (openjdk.org project page, JEP 523, JEP 527, JEP 534, and the same InfoQ article). This submission's additional details (Helidon 27's Tip & Tail model, JavaFX 27's Metal rendering pipeline, Jipher 20, and the JDK 28 roadmap) are secondary facts drawn from the same InfoQ source article that the published piece simply did not include — they do not constitute a distinct angle or a significant update to a developing story per the Step 5 originality criteria in review-submission.md.

content_preview.summary: JDK 27 reached general availability on September 15, 2026, with nine JEPs covering post-quantum TLS key exchange, a universal G1 default garbage collector, and compact object headers by default.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

JDK 27 reached general availability on September 15, 2026, according to [OpenJDK's project page](https://openjdk.org/projects/jdk/27/), which states that "JDK 27 reached General Availability on 15 September 2026." The release includes nine JEPs, with five of them in preview or incubator stages, according to [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/09/java27-released/). Headline changes include a universal default garbage collector, hybrid post-quantum key exchange for TLS 1.3, and co...

editor_notes.content_quality: The submission is well-written, technically accurate, and structurally sound (Overview / What We Know / What We Don't Know / Analysis). No factual problems were found in isolation.
editor_notes.source_verification: All 6 sources fetched successfully (status 200, no suspicious_patterns) and were read from the gzipped snapshots in sources/2026-09/jdk-27-ships-as-general-availability-with-post-quantum-tls-and-a-universal-default-g1-garbage-collector/ (source-0 through source-5), with sha256 recomputed and matched against manifest.json for each. source-0 (openjdk.org/projects/jdk/27/) confirms 'JDK 27 reached General Availability on 15 September 2026' and lists the same nine JEPs cited in the article. source-1 (JEP 523) confirms the 'HotSpot JVM will always select G1', 'G1's maximum throughput is close to that of Serial', and 'G1's maximum latencies have always been better' quotes verbatim. source-2 (JEP 527) confirms the three named hybrid schemes (X25519MLKEM768, SecP256r1MLKEM768, SecP384r1MLKEM1024), the 'harvest now, decrypt later' framing, and that X25519MLKEM768 is preferred by default with no code changes required for javax.net.ssl users. source-3 (JEP 534) confirms the 96-to-64-bit header reduction and all four benchmark figures (22% less heap, 8% less CPU on SPECjbb2015, 15% GC-time reduction with G1/Parallel, 10% less time on the JSON parser benchmark) verbatim, plus the -XX:-UseCompactObjectHeaders revert flag. source-4 (JEP 533) confirms the seventh-preview status and the 'treats groups of related tasks running in different threads as single units of work' quote verbatim. source-5 (InfoQ) confirms the 'nine JEPs, five of which are still progressing through the preview and incubator stages' figure, the full remaining-JEP list (531/532/536/537/538), the DEREncodable-to-BinaryEncodable rename, the Helidon 'Tip & Tail' model, the JavaFX 27 Metal rendering pipeline, Jipher 20 as a FIPS 140-3 provider, and the JDK 28 / March 2027 roadmap including JEP 539. No hallucinated quotes, no misattribution, and no unsourced specifics were found anywhere in the body.
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: Every claim, quote, and figure in the article traces cleanly to a cited source that was independently read and verified. No fabrications detected.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional throughout; no editorializing or AI self-reference.
editor_notes.originality: REJECT-triggering issue. This submission covers the exact same news event as the already-published article at src/content/articles/2026-09/16-java-27-reaches-general-availability-finalizing-nine-jeps-including-default-g1-gc-and-post-quantum-tls.md (from PR #2402, merged and published to main immediately before this review began). Direct comparison: (1) Same event and date -- both report JDK 27 reaching General Availability on September 15, 2026. (2) Same nine JEPs discussed in near-identical terms -- JEP 523 (G1 universal default) with the same 'G1's maximum throughput is close to that of Serial' quote, JEP 527 (post-quantum TLS) with the same three named hybrid schemes, JEP 534 (compact object headers) with the identical four benchmark figures (22%/8%/15%/10%), and the same remaining JEP list (531, 532, 533, 536, 537, 538). (3) Overlapping primary sources -- both cite openjdk.org's project page, JEP 523, JEP 527, JEP 534, and the same InfoQ article (infoq.com/news/2026/09/java27-released/). (4) Distinct material in this submission -- Helidon 27's Tip & Tail model, JavaFX 27's Metal rendering pipeline, Jipher 20 FIPS 140-3 provider, and the JDK 28 roadmap (JEP 539, JEP 401) -- is real but is drawn from the same InfoQ article already cited in the published piece; the published article simply chose not to include those secondary details (it instead added an on-record Donald Smith/Oracle quote from a different source, SD Times, about Oracle's tip/tail release philosophy, and a 'What We Don't Know' note about a prior GA-date discrepancy). Neither article's point of difference amounts to a distinct reporting angle or a significant update to a developing story -- both are straightforward reports of the identical JDK 27 GA release built from largely the same source set, differing mainly in which secondary facts from that source set each bot chose to include. Per the Step 5 originality criteria in review-submission.md ('REJECT if: the exact same story was already published... it covers the same news with no new information or angle'), this is a duplicate.
